text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me exactly where the wrist pain is located and when these symptoms first started? Also, have you noticed any joint stiffness or swelling in other parts of your body?

speaker: Patient
text: 17-year-old male. The patient presents with a 3-day history of pain in his left wrist, which worsened this morning accompanied by chills and malaise. He recounts having a self-resolving left knee pain the previous week. Reports recent return from a camping trip in Minnesota. Sexually active with one female partner. No history of trauma to the wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your recent camping trip in Minnesota, did you notice any tick bites or develop a circular, expanding rash on your skin? Have you also experienced any neurological symptoms like headaches, neck stiffness, or facial drooping?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pain in the left wrist. I also have Chills, Malaise, Painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on both wrists and hands, Swelling and erythema of the left wrist, Severe tenderness to palpation and passive movement of the left wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: The painless violaceous lesions on your hands and wrists are highly specific for meningococcemia, which is a medical emergency. text: Past medical history: Otherwise healthy with no significant past medical history. Social history: Admits to being sexually active with one female partner who uses a diaphragm for contraception. Recently went on a camping trip to Minnesota.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you have any signs of meningeal irritation, such as neck stiffness, severe headache, or sensitivity to light? I need to rule out meningitis as a complication of the suspected bacteremia.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies trauma to the wrist, reports a history of knee pain that resolved on its own. No other systemic symptoms mentioned.

speaker: Doctor
text: The history of migratory joint pain (knee then wrist) and the camping trip in Minnesota strongly suggest Lyme disease, specifically Lyme arthritis, despite the atypical description of the rash. The "violaceous vesiculopustular" description may be a misinterpretation of erythema migrans or a secondary infection, but the clinical picture of monoarticular arthritis after a tick-endemic exposure is classic. DIAGNOSIS READY: Lyme Arthritis
